message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Here's everything in order.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it, so the floor isn't flat across the joint. You can feel it with your foot or fingertips. It catches toes, collects dirt, and shows clearly when light comes across the floor low, for example from a window.

It's a particular risk with long tiles like your 30 × 60s, because they're often very slightly bowed in the middle. Two things help:
- **Use tile levelling clips.** These are cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.
- **Offset each row by no more than a third of a tile**, not by half. With bowed tiles, a half offset puts the high middle of one tile against the low ends of the next.

## Grout colour

Go for a **mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. It hides everyday dirt far better than white or very pale grout, and it still looks clean against pale grey porcelain. Avoid very light grout on a floor; it's the main reason floors look dirty after a month.

For extra protection, use a stain-resistant grout, or seal ordinary cement grout once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first.** Tiling the whole floor before the toilet goes in means no fiddly cuts around the base of the toilet, and the toilet sits on the finished floor at the right height. It also makes the toilet easier to replace later. Just check that the soil pipe connection will line up with the new floor height.

## How many boxes

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so you need **24 tiles** to cover the floor exactly
- Adding 10%: 26.4, so **27 tiles**
- Boxes of 8: **buy 4 boxes** (32 tiles)

Three boxes would give exactly 24 tiles with nothing spare, which isn't enough. Grout gaps mean the tiles won't fit the room perfectly whole, so some will need cutting, and you'll want spares for mistakes. The 5 spare tiles are worth keeping after you finish, in case one ever cracks. Check that all four boxes have the same batch number so the colour matches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, roughly 9 till 12, so there'll be some noise. Sorry about that, and thank you for being so patient with the skip on the drive these past two weeks. It'll be gone soon, I promise!
>
> Thanks again,
> [Name]

## Three tips for your first floor

1. **Preparation is most of the job.** The floor underneath must be flat, solid and clean. If it's floorboards, it will need overboarding with plywood or tile backer board first, because tiles crack on a floor that flexes. Before mixing any adhesive, lay the tiles out dry to plan where the cuts will fall. Aim for cuts at the edges that are at least half a tile, not thin slivers by the door.
2. **Get full adhesive coverage.** For 30 × 60 tiles, use a 10–12 mm notched trowel. Spread a thin layer on the back of each tile as well as on the floor (called "back-buttering"). Mix the adhesive in small batches, because it starts to set as you work. Every so often, lift a freshly laid tile to check the back is fully covered. Hollow spots crack later.
3. **Go slowly, and finish at the door.** Practise a few cuts on a spare tile first. Work from the far side of the room back towards the doorway so you don't box yourself in. Then keep off the floor for at least 24 hours before grouting.

You're right that the videos make it look easier than it is. It's a small, simple-shaped room, though, which is a good first project. Good luck!
